findings.title: Google credential key is overwritten with a `{success, data}` wrapper on every token refresh
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the zod `safeParse` result object, not the parsed data. Before this change, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(...)` returned the token itself. Now `key` is `{ success: true, data: {...} }`, and that object is written to `credential.key`. This happens in the default (non-sync) path too, so it affects every Google Calendar user. After the first refresh, the next `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` in the constructor throws, and the Google Calendar integration stops working for that user. Store `key.data`, or have the helper return the data.

findings.title: Minimum token schema strips every field except access_token
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]` is not a pattern key. `ZodString.toString()` returns "[object Object]", so both computed keys are the same literal property "[object Object]" and the second overwrites the first. The effective schema is `{access_token: string, "[object Object]"?: unknown}` in zod's default strip mode. In sync mode every other property is therefore dropped: expiry_date, expires_in, scope, token_type, instance_url, etc. The consequences differ per app. Zoom computes `expiry_date` from an undefined `expires_in` (NaN, stored as null), so the next `zoomTokenSchema.parse` fails. Salesforce loses `instance_url`. Google loses `expiry_date`, `scope` and `token_type`. Use `.passthrough()` or `z.record`/`.catchall` with an explicit expiry field.

findings.title: Placeholder "refresh_token" overwrites the real refresh token in the default path
findings.body: The fallback `refresh_token = "refresh_token"` also runs when sync is disabled. Office365's `refreshTokenResponseSchema` makes `refresh_token` optional, and the caller spreads `tokenResponse.data` over the stored credentials. Previously, if Microsoft omitted a refresh_token, the existing one was kept. Now it is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token", and every later refresh fails permanently. Only inject the placeholder in sync mode, or don't inject it at all.

findings.title: Sync path returns a raw fetch Response that callers expecting provider-specific objects can't use
findings.body:
In sync mode the helper returns a WHATWG `Response`. In native mode it returns whatever `refreshFunction` returns, so callers get a different type depending on the mode. Several callers break in sync mode:
- Google Calendar reads `res?.data`, which is undefined on a Response, so `token.access_token` throws. The error is swallowed and the expired token keeps being used.
- Zoho Bigin and ZohoCRM read `tokenInfo.data.error`, the axios shape, and throw a TypeError.
- HubSpot treats the result as a token object (`expiresIn`, `accessToken`), computes a NaN expiry and stores the Response object as the credential key.

The helper should normalize the result, e.g. parse JSON and return a common token shape, or the callers must branch on mode.

findings.title: Credential id passed as the Cal.com user id to the sync endpoint
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` passes `credential.id` where the helper expects `userId`. The sync endpoint receives `calcomUserId=<credential id>`. It will return tokens for whichever user happens to have that id, or for nobody. In the first case one user's Zoho tokens get written into another user's credential. Team credentials (userId null) are also sent to the sync endpoint, against the helper's stated intent. Pass `credential.userId` here.

findings.title: appStoreMetadata is indexed by slug, but it is keyed by app directory name
findings.body: `appStoreMetadata` is generated keyed by app directory name (e.g. `googlecalendar`, `zoomvideo`, `office365calendar`), not by slug. Looking it up with `app.slug` (`google-calendar`, `zoom`, `office365-calendar`, `msteams`) returns undefined, so the webhook answers 404 for most of the OAuth apps this PR targets. It only works by accident where slug equals dirName. Select `dirName` from the App row and index by that.

findings.title: `prisma` used without being imported
findings.body: The new `prisma.credential.update(...)` call references `prisma`, but this file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. At best it resolves to the dev-only `globalThis.prisma`. In production that global is not set, so this throws a ReferenceError/TypeError. Since `getClient` runs in the constructor, every Salesforce booking/CRM operation fails.

findings.title: Salesforce refreshes the token on every instantiation, then ignores the new token
findings.body: `getClient` now unconditionally POSTs to the Salesforce token endpoint every time the service is constructed, with no expiry check. That adds latency and rate-limit pressure on every booking. Afterwards the `jsforce.Connection` is still built with the old `credentialKey.access_token` and `instance_url` instead of the freshly refreshed values, so the extra request achieves nothing for the current call. The URL is also hardcoded to `login.salesforce.com`, which breaks sandbox orgs. This refresh also bypasses `refreshOAuthTokens` while still using the sync-mode schema, which corrupts the stored key (see the schema stripping issue).

findings.title: Success is detected via `statusText === "OK"`
findings.body: `statusText` is empty for HTTP/2 responses and is not guaranteed to be "OK" for a 200, so a successful refresh can be reported as a 400 error. Use `response.ok`. Also, the `!accessTokenParsed.success` branch below is dead, because `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws on failure instead of returning success=false.

findings.title: Zoom sends app slug "zoomvideo" instead of "zoom"
findings.body: Zoom's app slug and appId is "zoom" (see `createOAuthAppCredential({ appId: "zoom" ...})` in the callback). The webhook also identifies apps by slug. The refresh call sends `appSlug=zoomvideo`, the directory name, so the self-hoster's sync endpoint gets an identifier that doesn't match what it uses for the webhook. Zoom refreshes will fail or return the wrong app's tokens.

findings.title: Webex, Lark and MS Teams still require the provider-native response shape in sync mode
findings.body: Webex validates the response with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema` directly, which requires a scope literal, token_type, refresh_token and refresh_token_expires_in. Lark runs it through `handleLarkError`, which expects `{code:0,data:{...}}`. MS Teams overwrites the entire stored key with the response. All three are routed to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, whose documented contract is "only the access token and expiry date". With a conforming endpoint, Webex rejects every refresh, Lark throws, and Teams loses its refresh_token. The endpoint contract is not consistent across the integrations this PR switches over.

findings.title: Outbound sync request carries no authentication
findings.body: Cal.com POSTs only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` to the sync endpoint, with no shared secret, signature or encryption. The inbound webhook, by contrast, requires a secret and AES-encrypted keys. The self-hoster's endpoint therefore has no way to verify that the caller is Cal.com. Anyone who can reach it can enumerate user ids and obtain live third-party access tokens. Send the webhook secret or an HMAC header, and ideally encrypt the response with the shared key. Also check `response.ok` before returning.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==`
findings.body: The secret is compared with `!==`, which leaks timing information. If the header is sent more than once it becomes a `string[]` and never matches. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on the buffers after checking the lengths. The endpoint also accepts any HTTP method.

findings.title: Malformed body or bad ciphertext returns an unhandled 500
findings.body: `schema.parse`, `symmetricDecrypt` and `JSON.parse` all throw on bad input, and nothing catches them. The caller gets a generic 500 instead of a 400 explaining what was wrong. The decrypted keys are also stored without any validation against the app's credential schema.

findings.title: Updating a credential via the webhook doesn't clear `invalid`
findings.body: Google, Zoom and Webex set `invalid: true` on invalid_grant. When the parent app later pushes fresh keys through this webhook, only `key` is updated. The credential stays flagged invalid and is still treated as broken. Reset `invalid: false` on update.

findings.title: Removed diagnostic logging of the Microsoft refresh error
findings.body: The old code logged the zod error and the raw Microsoft response when parsing failed. Now `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws a generic "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" and the MS error body is lost. That makes Outlook token problems much harder to debug. The behavior also changed from "keep the old token and continue" to "throw".

findings.title: No tests for the new refresh/sync helpers or the webhook
findings.body: The PR changes token refresh for about ten integrations and adds a credential-writing webhook, and it states that no tests were added or run. Unit tests for `parseRefreshTokenResponse` would have caught several of the issues above: the returned wrapper object, the fields stripped by the broken schema, and the placeholder refresh_token. The same goes for `refreshOAuthTokens` (sync vs native return types) and the webhook (slug→metadata lookup).
